newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Iliescu forecasts win, says Romania on right path.
newsitem.headline: Iliescu forecasts win, says Romania on right path.

text.p: President Ion Iliescu, predicting victory in next weekend's election, said Romania had chosen the correct path to post-communist reforms despite problems which had left it behind its neighbours.
"I am (confident)," he said in an interview during a stop on Saturday in a village 100 km (60 miles) west of Bucharest.

"I have this feeling, the general feeling of the people. In spite of the difficulties our society is passing through there is confidence that Romania chose the right route during the (1989) revolution."
The latest opinion poll gave 36.5 percent of the vote to Iliescu, well in front of 15 rivals but short of the 50 percent needed for outright first-round victory.

His Party for Social Democracy (PDSR) lies second in polls for parliamentary elections. It is generally conceded that a coalition will have to govern the country seven years after the execution of communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu.
Iliescu said Romania was now mature enough to cope with a "cohabitation" between a president backed by a leftist party and parliament dominated by an expected centrist majority.
"I think that in the last two years there is a more realistic approach and feeling of the stability which does exist in Romania, which is a factor of stability," he said.

Iliescu, a former communist, won presidential elections in 1990 and 1992. He draws much of his support from rural areas, though residents of Topoloveni, a town of 10,000 people, gave him no more than a polite reception.
He two most serious two challengers, academic Emil Constantinescu and former prime minister Petre Roman, accuse him of failing to pursue market reforms seriously and plunging millions into poverty.

Iliescu denied that the gap between Romania and its neighbours had widened since 1989, despite statistics showing incomes to be about one-third those in Poland, which chose a fast-track approach to reform.
"I don't think the gap is increasing between us and other countries in central Europe. We do have a handicap to be overcome in the coming years," he said.
"I don't think Poland did fast, shock therapy. There was an attempt to do it, some inspiration from abroad...but even they didn't consider it a realistic approach."

Romania, he said, faced the additional difficulty of having paid off foreign debts under Ceausescu, paradoxically making contacts with Western banks more difficult. Its only sources of credit had been big Western institutions, led by the International Monetary Fund.
"Poland and Hungary, in particular, had open doors to the commercial bank network. Romania did not have even this chance because of the lack of foreign debt," he said.
"And in the beginning of the 1990s, commercial banks were not in a position to accept new clients. Only this year for the first time, we have entered into touch with these banks."
